razors.title: Type 1 / Type 2 decisions
razors.statement: One-way doors deserve deliberation; two-way doors deserve speed, and most doors are two-way.

razors.title: Disagree and commit
razors.statement: Argue hard before the decision, then execute as if you had won the argument.
razors.source: Andy Grove, Intel; formalised as an Amazon leadership principle

razors.title: Chesterton's fence
razors.statement: Do not remove a fence until you know why it was put there.

razors.title: YAGNI
razors.statement: Build it when you need it, not when you foresee needing it — foresight is usually wrong and always expensive.
razors.source: Kent Beck and Ron Jeffries, Extreme Programming

razors.title: The rule of three
razors.statement: Duplicate twice; abstract on the third occurrence, when you can finally see the shape.
razors.source: Martin Fowler, Refactoring (1999), crediting Don Roberts

razors.title: Gall's Law
razors.statement: A complex system that works evolved from a simple system that worked; one designed complex from scratch does not.

razors.title: Goodhart's Law
razors.statement: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
razors.source: Charles Goodhart (1975); phrasing by Marilyn Strathern (1997)

razors.title: Campbell's Law
razors.statement: The more a social indicator is used for decisions, the more it distorts the process it was meant to monitor.

razors.title: What would have to be true?
razors.statement: Stop arguing about which option is right and ask what the world would have to look like for each to be right.

razors.title: Hamming's question
razors.statement: What are the important problems in your field, and why are you not working on them?

razors.title: Cynefin
razors.statement: Match the method to the domain: clear, complicated, complex and chaotic problems each need a different move.

razors.title: The OODA loop
razors.statement: Observe, orient, decide, act — and win by cycling faster than the situation changes, not by deciding better.

razors.title: Second-order thinking
razors.statement: Ask 'and then what?' — the first consequence is rarely the one that decides whether it was a good idea.
razors.source: Howard Marks, The Most Important Thing (2011)

razors.title: Sunk cost
razors.statement: What you already spent is not a reason to continue; only the remaining cost and benefit are.

razors.title: Regret minimisation
razors.statement: For decisions at the scale of years, choose what you would least regret at eighty rather than what optimises now.

razors.title: KISS
razors.statement: Design so it can be repaired under pressure by someone who did not build it.

razors.title: Occam's razor
razors.statement: Prefer the explanation that needs the fewest assumptions — in debugging, the boring cause is usually the cause.

razors.title: Hanlon's razor
razors.statement: Never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by missing context.

razors.title: Parkinson's Law
razors.statement: Work expands to fill the time available, which is why deadlines shape scope more than estimates do.

razors.title: Hofstadter's Law
razors.statement: It always takes longer than you expect, even when you account for Hofstadter's Law.

razors.title: The Pareto principle
razors.statement: Roughly 80% of the effect comes from 20% of the causes — find that 20% before optimising anything.
razors.source: Vilfredo Pareto; named by Joseph Juran

razors.title: Conway's Law
razors.statement: A system's architecture mirrors the communication structure of the organisation that built it.

razors.title: The inverse Conway manoeuvre
razors.statement: If the architecture follows the org chart, change the org chart to get the architecture you want.
razors.source: Jonny LeRoy and Matt Simons, ThoughtWorks

razors.title: Hyrum's Law
razors.statement: With enough users, every observable behaviour of your system is depended on by somebody, regardless of what you promised.
razors.source: Hyrum Wright, Google; Software Engineering at Google

razors.title: Brooks's Law
razors.statement: Adding people to a late project makes it later, because communication paths grow faster than hands do.

razors.title: Essential vs accidental complexity
razors.statement: Tools only ever remove accidental complexity; the essential difficulty of the problem is untouched, so no single change gives an order of magnitude.

razors.title: Amdahl's Law
razors.statement: Speedup is capped by the fraction you did not parallelise — optimise the bottleneck or do not bother.

razors.title: Gustafson's Law
razors.statement: Amdahl's ceiling lifts when the problem grows with the machine — scale the work, not just the workers.

razors.title: Little's Law
razors.statement: Items in a system equal arrival rate times time spent — which is why cutting work-in-progress cuts latency.

razors.title: The Universal Scalability Law
razors.statement: Contention flattens your scaling curve and coherency bends it downward — past some node count, adding capacity loses throughput.

razors.title: Postel's Law, and its retraction
razors.statement: Be liberal in what you accept was protocol doctrine for forty years; RFC 9413 walked it back because tolerance ossifies protocols.
razors.source: Jon Postel, RFC 761 (1980); retracted in RFC 9413 (2023)

razors.title: The end-to-end argument
razors.statement: Put function at the endpoints; the network cannot guarantee correctness the endpoints must check anyway.

razors.title: Fallacies of distributed computing
razors.statement: The network is not reliable, latency is not zero, bandwidth is not infinite, and topology always changes.
razors.source: Peter Deutsch and James Gosling, Sun Microsystems

razors.title: The tail at scale
razors.statement: Fan out to enough services and the slowest one becomes your median — p99 of a part is p50 of the whole.
razors.source: Jeffrey Dean & Luiz André Barroso, CACM (2013)

razors.title: The law of leaky abstractions
razors.statement: All non-trivial abstractions leak, so the layer you were promised you could ignore is the one you will debug.

razors.title: Kernighan's Law
razors.statement: Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code — so code at your limit and you cannot debug it.
razors.source: Brian Kernighan, The Elements of Programming Style

razors.title: Lehman's laws of software evolution
razors.statement: A used system must keep changing or become less useful, and each change raises its complexity unless work is spent reducing it.

razors.title: Tesler's Law
razors.statement: Complexity is conserved: whatever you refuse to handle in the system gets handled by the user.

razors.title: Linus's Law, and its limits
razors.statement: Given enough eyeballs all bugs are shallow — but Heartbleed showed eyeballs must actually be looking.
razors.source: Eric S. Raymond, The Cathedral and the Bazaar (1997)

razors.title: Metcalfe's Law
razors.statement: A network's value grows with the square of its nodes, which is why the second user is worth more than the first.

razors.title: CAP and PACELC
razors.statement: Under a partition, choose consistency or availability; else, choose latency or consistency — the second half is the daily one.
razors.source: Eric Brewer (2000); Gilbert & Lynch (2002); Daniel Abadi (2010)

razors.title: Dunbar's number
razors.statement: Stable relationships cap out around 150, which is why organisations need structure at that size rather than more goodwill.

razors.title: The Peter principle
razors.statement: People rise to their level of incompetence, because promotion rewards the previous job rather than the next one.

razors.title: Software entropy
razors.statement: One broken window signals nobody is watching, and decay accelerates from there.

razors.title: The boy scout rule
razors.statement: Leave the code cleaner than you found it, in small increments nobody has to schedule.

razors.title: Separation of concerns
razors.statement: Study one aspect at a time, so each can be reasoned about without holding the others in your head.

razors.title: SOLID, and its critics
razors.statement: Five object-oriented principles worth knowing by name — and worth knowing that Dan North's CUPID argues they optimise the wrong thing.
razors.source: Robert C. Martin; acronym by Michael Feathers; critique by Dan North

razors.title: The wrong abstraction
razors.statement: Duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction — prefer copying to a shared thing that fits neither caller.
razors.source: Sandi Metz (2016); AHA by Kent C. Dodds

razors.title: The law of Demeter
razors.statement: Talk to your immediate collaborators only; a chain of dots is a dependency on someone else's internals.

razors.title: Composition over inheritance
razors.statement: Inheritance couples you to a parent's decisions forever; composition lets you change your mind.

razors.title: The strangler fig
razors.statement: Replace a legacy system by routing traffic away from it piece by piece, never by a rewrite-and-switch.

razors.title: Sacrificial architecture
razors.statement: Build knowing you will throw it away — designing for a lifespan you will not reach costs more than the rewrite.

razors.title: Bounded context
razors.statement: The same word means different things to different teams; draw the boundary where the meaning changes.

razors.title: CQRS and event sourcing
razors.statement: Separating reads from writes buys independent scaling and costs eventual consistency — and is wrong for most systems.

razors.title: The twelve-factor app
razors.statement: Config in the environment, processes stateless and disposable, dev and prod as alike as you can make them.

razors.title: Make it work, make it right, make it fast
razors.statement: In that order — each stage is cheaper when the one before it is done.

razors.title: Premature optimisation, quoted in full
razors.statement: Knuth said forget small efficiencies about 97% of the time — and immediately added that we must not pass up the critical 3%.
razors.source: Donald Knuth, 'Structured Programming with go to Statements' (1974)

razors.title: Simple made easy
razors.statement: Simple means unentangled; easy means familiar. Choosing easy over simple is how systems become impossible to change.

razors.title: Worse is better
razors.statement: A simpler, less complete design often wins, because it ships, spreads, and gets fixed in the field.

razors.title: The rule of least power
razors.statement: Choose the least powerful language that solves the problem — weaker formats are easier to analyse and outlive their authors.

razors.title: Circuit breaker and bulkhead
razors.statement: Stop calling a failing dependency, and partition resources so one saturated pool cannot take the process with it.

razors.title: Crash-only software
razors.statement: If the only way to stop is to crash, recovery is exercised constantly instead of on the worst night of the year.

razors.title: Backpressure over buffering
razors.statement: A queue that absorbs overload converts a throughput problem into a latency problem and hides it until it is worse.

razors.title: Idempotency keys
razors.statement: Exactly-once delivery does not exist; make the operation safe to repeat and at-least-once becomes enough.

razors.title: Immutable infrastructure
razors.statement: Replace servers rather than patching them, so what is running always matches what was described.

razors.title: Hexagonal architecture
razors.statement: Push the database and the UI to the edges as adapters, so the domain can be tested without either.

razors.title: Design for failure
razors.statement: Everything fails all the time — so ask what happens when this dependency is down, not whether it will be.

razors.title: Choose Boring Technology
razors.statement: Every team gets a small budget of innovation tokens; spend them where the novelty is the product.

razors.title: The four DORA keys
razors.statement: Deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore predict performance better than anything teams usually track.

razors.title: Continuous delivery
razors.statement: Keep the software releasable at all times; batching changes makes each release riskier, not safer.

razors.title: Trunk-based development
razors.statement: Long-lived branches defer integration pain rather than removing it; merge daily and hide incomplete work behind flags.

razors.title: Error budgets
razors.statement: 100% is the wrong reliability target; pick a number, and spend the gap on shipping instead of arguing.

razors.title: The toil budget
razors.statement: Cap manual, repetitive, automatable work at half a team's time, or operations eats all of engineering.

razors.title: Blameless postmortems
razors.statement: People act reasonably given what they knew; asking who erred buys silence, asking what made it look right buys information.

razors.title: Five whys, and why not
razors.statement: Asking why five times yields a single tidy cause for an event that had many — linear chains flatter the investigator.
razors.source: Taiichi Ohno, Toyota; critique by John Allspaw

razors.title: You build it, you run it
razors.statement: Carrying the pager for your own code is the fastest feedback loop in software.

razors.title: Deploy is not release
razors.statement: Ship the code dark and turn it on separately, so deployment risk and product risk stop being the same event.

razors.title: Progressive delivery
razors.statement: Expose a change to a growing slice of traffic, so the blast radius is a dial rather than a coin flip.

razors.title: The four golden signals
razors.statement: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation — if you can only have four dashboards, have these.

razors.title: The RED method
razors.statement: For every service: request rate, error rate, duration. Three metrics, uniform across everything you run.

razors.title: The USE method
razors.statement: For every resource: utilisation, saturation, errors — the checklist that finds the bottleneck rather than describing the symptom.

razors.title: The test pyramid, and the trophy
razors.statement: Many fast unit tests under fewer slow end-to-end ones — though Dodds argues integration tests deserve the widest band.
razors.source: Mike Cohn (2009); critique by Kent C. Dodds

razors.title: The defect cost curve
razors.statement: A bug costs more the later it is found — directionally true, though the famous 100x figure is not well supported.

razors.title: Chaos engineering
razors.statement: Inject the failure deliberately in daylight, because the alternative is discovering it at 3am.

razors.title: Theory of constraints
razors.statement: Any improvement not at the bottleneck is an illusion; find the constraint, exploit it, then subordinate everything else.

razors.title: Cost of delay
razors.statement: Price a week of lateness and prioritisation stops being an argument about opinions.
razors.source: Donald Reinertsen, Principles of Product Development Flow (2009)

razors.title: WIP limits
razors.statement: Starting less finishes more — by Little's Law, cutting work in progress cuts cycle time directly.

razors.title: Two-pizza teams
razors.statement: If a team cannot be fed by two pizzas, its coordination cost has begun to exceed its output.

razors.title: The single-threaded owner
razors.statement: One person whose only job is this initiative — shared ownership of a hard thing means nobody owns it.

razors.title: Production readiness review
razors.statement: A service earns the right to page you: runbooks, alerts, dashboards, and an owner, before it takes traffic.

razors.title: Appetite over estimate
razors.statement: Fix the time and vary the scope: ask how much this is worth, not how long it will take.

razors.title: BLUF
razors.statement: Bottom line up front: the first sentence carries the conclusion and the ask.

razors.title: The pyramid principle
razors.statement: One governing claim, a few points that each independently support it, evidence beneath those.

razors.title: SCQA
razors.statement: Situation, complication, question, answer — four sentences that make a reader want the recommendation before you give it.

razors.title: The inverted pyramid
razors.statement: Write so an editor can cut from the bottom without losing anything essential.

razors.title: Grice's maxims
razors.statement: Be as informative as needed, truthful, relevant and clear — most bad writing violates exactly one of the four.

razors.title: The curse of knowledge
razors.statement: Once you know something you cannot model not knowing it, which is why your context reads as throat-clearing.
razors.source: Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber (1989); Heath & Heath, Made to Stick

razors.title: The ladder of inference
razors.statement: You climb from data to conclusion in one step and forget the climb — disagreements are usually about rungs, not conclusions.

razors.title: Advocacy vs inquiry
razors.statement: State your reasoning and ask for theirs; pure advocacy produces winners rather than decisions.

razors.title: Situation-behaviour-impact
razors.statement: Name when it happened, what was done, and what followed — never the character trait you inferred.

razors.title: Nonviolent communication
razors.statement: Observation, feeling, need, request — separating what happened from what you made it mean.

razors.title: Radical candor
razors.statement: Care personally and challenge directly; dropping either gives you ruinous empathy or obnoxious aggression.

razors.title: Nemawashi
razors.statement: Socialise a decision one-to-one before the meeting, so the meeting confirms rather than discovers.

razors.title: The narrative memo
razors.statement: Six pages of prose read in silence beats slides, because narrative exposes gaps that bullets hide.

razors.title: Write to decide, or write to inform
razors.statement: Say which one this document is in the first line; a reader who guesses wrong reads it uselessly.
razors.source: Design-doc practice at Google, Uber, Oxide

razors.title: The staff archetypes
razors.statement: Tech lead, architect, solver, right hand — four shapes of the same level, and organisations need different ones.

razors.title: Glue work
razors.statement: The invisible coordination that holds projects together is essential, uncredited, and a career built only on it stalls.

razors.title: The trust equation
razors.statement: Credibility plus reliability plus intimacy, divided by self-orientation — the denominator is what most people get wrong.

razors.title: Influence without authority
razors.statement: Find the currency the other person values and trade in it; authority is one currency among many.

razors.title: Crucial conversations
razors.statement: When stakes and emotion are high, restore safety before content — nobody hears an argument they feel attacked by.

razors.title: Working backwards
razors.statement: Write the press release and the FAQ first; if you cannot make it sound compelling, do not build it.

razors.title: RFC culture
razors.statement: Make the design reviewable in writing before it is built, so disagreement is cheap and recorded.
razors.source: Google design docs; Rust RFCs; Oxide RFDs

razors.title: DACI
razors.statement: Driver, approver, contributors, informed — naming the approver is what stops a decision drifting.

razors.title: Mentorship vs sponsorship
razors.statement: A mentor talks to you; a sponsor talks about you in rooms you are not in. Only one changes your trajectory.

razors.title: Crossing the chasm, internally
razors.statement: Internal adoption follows the same curve as products — win the early adopters, then the pragmatists who want proof.

razors.title: The andon cord
razors.statement: Anyone can stop the line — and it only works if pulling it is celebrated rather than investigated.

razors.title: Context, not control
razors.statement: If someone makes a bad call, ask what context they were missing before reaching for a process.

razors.title: The bar raiser
razors.statement: Give one person outside the hiring team a veto, so urgency cannot quietly lower the standard.

razors.title: Strong opinions, weakly held — and its failure
razors.statement: Intended as a forecasting discipline; in practice it licenses confident noise, because the strong half is louder than the weak half.

razors.title: Bus factor
razors.statement: Count how many people can be lost before the project stops — if the answer is one, that is the top risk.

razors.title: Situational leadership
razors.statement: Match direction to competence and confidence: the same support that helps a novice insults an expert.

razors.title: Scope is granted, not claimed
razors.statement: You earn larger scope by handling problems slightly larger than the ones you were given, visibly.
razors.source: Will Larson; Tanya Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path

razors.title: Managing up is informing, not asking
razors.statement: Bring the decision you are about to make and the reasoning behind it, not the question.

razors.title: The cost asymmetry in hiring
razors.statement: A false positive costs a team a year; a false negative costs one good candidate. Optimise accordingly.
razors.source: Widespread hiring practice; Amazon bar-raiser rationale

razors.title: Psychological safety
razors.statement: The strongest predictor of team performance is whether people can admit mistakes without fear.
